<reason>PRO opened with a strong intuitive and normative case (real money, "Buy" button misrepresentation, contracts cannot nullify succession) and a plausible administrative mechanism. But CON systematically converted PRO's own repairs into liabilities. The pivotal move was CON's exploitation of PRO's "one seat" concession in [A2.1]: CON showed the resulting entitlement is unsplittable and, crucially in [B4.3]-[B4.4], unsaleable, so probate's normal answer for indivisible assets (sell and split value) is unavailable — meaning two of three heirs get nothing, which hollows out the very emotional case PRO opened with. CON also caught the slippage from the motion's "next of kin" to "the estate's designee," and though PRO's A1 (intestacy defaults yield to wills) was a competent, honest answer, it partly conceded that CON's chosen-beneficiary framing was doing the work. The heaviest blow was PRO's freely offered admission in [A4.3] that "the heir's claim dies with the entity," which CON crystallized into the memorable and genuinely decisive comparison: a file the buyer holds versus "a receipt for a promise." CON's answer to PRO's best pressure question was also the sharpest exchange of the debate — the rivalry/DRM-free reframe explained why mandated transferability differs in kind from a death-triggered mandate, and why the motion only does work precisely where the license remains permanent. PRO's late reframe (CON's remedy is a larger intervention and not the motion) was its best closing thrust and had real force, but CON answered it directly: both legislate against the licence, so the test is what the statute leaves behind. Add two clipped PRO turns and a mild misdescription of CON conceding the diaries point, and CON built the cleaner, better-weighed route to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B4.3]-[B4.5]: answering PRO's indivisibility question by noting probate divides indivisible assets by selling them, then showing the motion's asset is by definition unsaleable — combined with weaponizing PRO's own admission that "the heir's claim dies with the entity" — turned PRO's remedy into one relative, one server, no market, no residue.</best_rebuttal>
